title: How can we find three angles when only one is known?
description: Two lines cross with one angle of one hundred and twenty degrees known. Each next angle is found by going round the crossing and taking the last angle away from one hundred and eighty, with no measuring. Keeko doubts that all four angles are the same.
teaching_notes: One idea: each angle at a crossing is 180 take away its neighbour, because the two sit on a straight line. Watch for students who think all four angles are equal because they look alike.

source: Two lines cross. The angle a is 120°. Find b, c and d going round the point, without measuring.
video_script.why: The child uses the straight line of one hundred and eighty degrees to find the angles that are not given.
video_script.substitution: The book's own crossing with the angle eigh given as one hundred and twenty degrees, solved by going round it one neighbour at a time.
video_script.anchor: Two lines crossing, with the four angles named a, b, c and d going round the crossing and a marked 120°.
video_script.wrong_answer: every angle is one hundred and twenty degrees
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks all four angles are equal because they look alike.
video_script.payoff_line: Angle b is sixty degrees, angle c is one hundred and twenty degrees, angle d is sixty degrees.

final_answer.spoken: angle b is sixty degrees, angle c is one hundred and twenty degrees and angle d is sixty degrees

video_script.design: One crossing stays on the stage all video. Each linear pair lights up in turn as the working band builds line by line.

beats.on_screen: the small title card From your book appears; two lines cross; the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round the crossing, and a is 120°

marks.m1: the small title card From your book appears and two lines cross
marks.m2: the four angles are named a, b, c and d going round
marks.m3: a question mark appears in the anchor band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book about two lines that cross.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The four angles are named eigh, b, c and d going round the crossing.
<bookmark mark='m2b'/>The angle eigh is one hundred and twenty degrees, and we may not measure the others.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>How can we find the other three angles?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: two neighbouring angles lie along one straight line; a straight line is 180°; the pair is a linear pair

marks.m1: two neighbouring angles lie along one straight line
marks.m2: a straight line is marked as 180°
marks.m3: the pair is named a linear pair

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Two angles side by side on a straight line are called a linear pair.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A straight angle measures one hundred and eighty degrees.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A linear pair always adds up to one hundred and eighty degrees.

marks.m1: the given angle is written in the working band

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Given, the angle eigh is one hundred and twenty degrees.

beats.on_screen: To find: b, c and d, without measuring

marks.m1: the words to find are written under the given

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to find the angles b, c and d, without measuring.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: a + b = 180 (linear pair), so b = 180 - 120 = 60

marks.m1: the pair a and b lights up on the line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one. The angles eigh and b are a linear pair, so they add up to one hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Then b is one hundred and eighty take away one hundred and twenty, which is sixty.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: b + c = 180 (linear pair), so c = 180 - 60 = 120

marks.m1: the pair b and c lights up on the line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two. The angles b and c are a linear pair, so they add up to one hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Then c is one hundred and eighty take away sixty, which is one hundred and twenty.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: c + d = 180 (linear pair), so d = 180 - 120 = 60

marks.m1: the pair c and d lights up on the line

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three. The angles c and d are a linear pair, so they add up to one hundred and eighty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Then d is one hundred and eighty take away one hundred and twenty, which is sixty.

beats.on_screen: Answer: b = 60°, c = 120°, d = 60°; a and c are 120°, b and d are 60°

marks.m1: the three angles are written and boxed
marks.m2: the facing angles light up in pairs

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Angle b is sixty degrees, angle c is one hundred and twenty degrees, angle d is sixty degrees.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Facing angles are equal: eigh and c match, and b and d match.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the crossing
narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows all four angles as 120°; the angle next to a is drawn on the same straight line: 120 + 120 = 240; the claim is struck out

marks.m1: the bubble shows all four angles as 120°
marks.m2: the angle next to a is drawn on the same straight line with 120 + 120 = 240
marks.m3: the claim is struck out and b = 60° replaces it

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks every angle is one hundred and twenty degrees, because the angles look alike.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But eigh and b sit on one straight line. One hundred and twenty plus one hundred and twenty is two hundred and forty.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is more than one hundred and eighty, so b must be smaller.
